title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
ImportantSource material, not a specification



This compilation is working material. It restates inventory methods by category, with early coding notes, and is being replaced category by category by methodology narratives written to the Methodology Narrative Standard. Use it as raw material when writing a narrative. Do not cite it as the methodology, and do not add new categories or content to it.
When a category’s narrative is approved, its section here is marked as retired and points to the narrative.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
section: 1.1 Annex 2.1 – CO2 Emissions from Fossil Fuel Combustion
text:
1.1 Annex 2.1 – CO2 Emissions from Fossil Fuel Combustion
Overview. CO2 emissions from fossil fuel combustion are estimated using a bottom-up, sector-based approach aligned with the IPCC 2006 Guidelines Tier 2 method. The methodology begins with raw fuel consumption data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), applies a series of adjustments to arrive at energy consumed for combustion purposes, and then converts adjusted consumption to CO2 emissions using fuel-specific carbon content coefficients. The primary inputs are EIA fuel consumption statistics; the primary output is CO2 emissions in MMT CO2 Eq. by fuel type and end-use sector.


1.1.1 Step 1 – Determine total fuel consumption by fuel type and sector
Fuel consumption data are obtained from the EIA in physical units and converted to energy equivalents (TBtu, using higher heating values). Data are aggregated by end-use sector (residential, commercial, industrial, transportation, electric power, and U.S. Territories) and by primary and secondary fuel type. Electricity use is allocated to sectors based on EIA retail sales to ultimate customers. For years 2010 onward, electricity consumption by electric vehicles is estimated separately and reallocated from residential and commercial sectors to transportation.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
EIA Monthly Energy Review; EIA fuel consumption surveys by sector and fuel type; EIA electricity retail sales data; Browning (2018) EV electricity methodology


Outputs
Table of unadjusted fuel consumption (TBtu) by fuel type x sector x year


Key operations
Unit conversion (physical -> TBtu); aggregation by sector and fuel type; EV electricity reallocation from residential/commercial to transportation


R notes
dplyr::summarise() for aggregation; conversion factors stored as named constants or lookup table; EV reallocation applied conditionally for years >= 2010


Corresponding script
R/01_fuel_consumption_raw.R








1.1.2 Step 2 – Subtract uses accounted for in the IPPU chapter
Portions of seven fuel types (coking coal, distillate fuel, industrial other coal, petroleum coke, natural gas, residual fuel oil, and other oil >401 degreesF) are reallocated to the Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU) chapter because they are consumed as raw materials rather than as combustion fuels. These amounts are removed from Energy chapter totals to avoid double-counting with IPPU. The adjustment quantities are derived from activity data used in the relevant IPPU calculations (e.g., iron and steel production, aluminum production, ammonia production, carbon black, silicon carbide, titanium dioxide, ferroalloys).






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
IPPU activity data for iron & steel, aluminum, ammonia, carbon black, SiC, TiO2, ferroalloys; EIA reported coking coal consumption


Outputs
Adjustment table (TBtu) by fuel type to be subtracted from industrial sector totals


Key operations
Join IPPU-derived fuel quantities to energy consumption table; subtract adjustment amounts by fuel type


R notes
Left join on fuel type; negative values possible where IPPU consumption exceeds EIA-reported totals – handle with pmax() or explicit flag


Corresponding script
R/02_ippu_adjustments.R








1.1.3 Step 3 – Adjust for conversion of fossil fuels and exports
Three adjustments are applied. First, ethanol blended into motor gasoline is removed (biogenic carbon tracked in LULUCF, not Energy). Second, biodiesel and renewable diesel blended into distillate fuel oil are removed for the same reason (from 2009 onward). Third, industrial other coal used to produce synthetic natural gas at the Dakota Gasification Plant is adjusted: the energy content associated with CO2 exported to Canada by pipeline is subtracted from industrial other coal consumption, as that CO2 is not emitted to the U.S. atmosphere.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 3










Item
Detail




Inputs
EIA ethanol blending volumes; EIA biodiesel/renewable diesel volumes (2009+); Dakota Gasification Plant CO2 export volumes


Outputs
Further-adjusted consumption table with biofuel fractions and exported CO2 energy removed


Key operations
Conditional subtraction by year and fuel type; motor gasoline and distillate fuel oil adjusted separately


R notes
Year-conditional logic (if_else() or case_when()) for biodiesel adjustment start year; Dakota adjustment is a single small annual subtraction from industrial other coal


Corresponding script
R/03_biofuel_and_conversion_adjustments.R








1.1.4 Step 4 – Adjust sectoral allocation of distillate fuel oil and motor gasoline
EPA conducts an independent bottom-up analysis of transportation fuel consumption using Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) data. Where FHWA estimates differ from EIA’s sectoral allocation, the transportation sector’s distillate and motor gasoline consumption is adjusted to match the FHWA-derived figure. Because EIA national totals are considered accurate, the difference is redistributed proportionally across the residential, commercial, and industrial sectors.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 4










Item
Detail




Inputs
FHWA Highway Statistics (annual); EIA sectoral distillate and motor gasoline consumption


Outputs
Revised distillate and motor gasoline consumption by sector, with transportation adjusted to FHWA estimate


Key operations
Calculate difference between FHWA and EIA transportation figures; redistribute difference proportionally across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors


R notes
Proportional redistribution: non-transport sector shares calculated from unadjusted values, then applied to the adjustment delta


Corresponding script
R/04_fhwa_sectoral_adjustment.R








1.1.5 Step 5 – Subtract consumption for non-energy use
Fossil fuels consumed for non-energy purposes (e.g., asphalt, lubricants, plastics feedstocks) are subtracted from total fuel consumption. These fuels sequester varying fractions of their carbon content in products rather than releasing it to the atmosphere during combustion. Their emissions are estimated separately in the Carbon Emitted from Non-Energy Uses of Fossil Fuels section.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 5










Item
Detail




Inputs
EIA non-energy use estimates by fuel type and sector (Table A-18)


Outputs
Consumption table with non-energy fuel quantities removed


Key operations
Subtract non-energy use volumes by fuel type from total consumption


R notes
Non-energy use table joined by fuel type and year; subtraction produces the combustion-only consumption figures


Corresponding script
R/05_non_energy_use_adjustment.R








1.1.6 Step 6 – Subtract consumption of international bunker fuels
Emissions from international transport (aviation jet fuel, marine residual and distillate fuel oil used in international shipping) are excluded from national totals per IPCC and UNFCCC guidelines. The estimated bunker fuel volumes are subtracted from EIA transportation sector consumption figures. Bunker fuel emissions are reported separately.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 6










Item
Detail




Inputs
International bunker fuel estimates by fuel type (Table A-19); see also Annex 3.3 for aviation methodology


Outputs
Final adjusted consumption table (TBtu), equivalent to Tables A-5 through A-17 in the Annex


Key operations
Subtract bunker volumes from transportation sector jet fuel, residual fuel, and distillate fuel entries


R notes
Straightforward subtraction; bunker fuel table joined by fuel type and year


Corresponding script
R/06_bunker_fuel_adjustment.R








1.1.7 Step 7 – Determine the carbon content of all fuels
Adjusted energy consumption (TBtu) for each fuel type is multiplied by a fuel-specific carbon content coefficient (MMT C/QBtu) to yield the carbon content of combusted fuels. Coefficients are sourced from EIA and EPA and largely reflect U.S.-specific fuel qualities rather than IPCC defaults. For several fuels (motor gasoline, distillate, HGL, natural gas, crude oil, motor gasoline blending components), coefficients vary annually to reflect changes in fuel composition. For geothermal electricity generation, carbon content is estimated from net generation by geotype (flash steam, dry steam, binary) multiplied by geotype-specific coefficients.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 7










Item
Detail




Inputs
Adjusted fuel consumption by fuel type and sector (Steps 1-6 output); carbon content coefficient table (Table A-20), annually variable for select fuels


Outputs
Carbon content (MMT C) by fuel type and sector


Key operations
Join adjusted consumption to carbon content coefficients by fuel type and year; multiply consumption x coefficient; geothermal handled separately by geotype


R notes
Annual variability in coefficients means the join must be on both fuel_type and year; fixed coefficients can be stored as a lookup; variable ones require a time-series table


Corresponding script
R/07_carbon_content.R








1.1.8 Step 8 – Estimate CO2 emissions
Carbon content values are converted to CO2 emissions by applying a 100 percent oxidation fraction (per IPCC 2006 guidance). Emissions are expressed in MMT CO2 Eq. and summarised by major fuel type and consuming sector. To report emissions by final end-use sector, electric power sector emissions are distributed to residential, commercial, industrial, and transportation sectors in proportion to each sector’s share of aggregate electricity consumption. Transportation emissions are further disaggregated by vehicle type and mode using fuel consumption data by vehicle type (see Annex 3.1).






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 8










Item
Detail




Inputs
Carbon content by fuel type and sector (Step 7); electricity consumption by end-use sector (Table A-22); transportation fuel consumption by vehicle type (Annex 3.1)


Outputs
CO2 emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.) by fuel type x sector; also by final end-use sector with electric power distributed; transportation sub-allocated by vehicle/mode


Key operations
Multiply C content x (44/12) to convert C to CO2; allocate electric power emissions to end-use sectors by electricity share; join transport mode allocation factors


R notes
C-to-CO2 conversion factor is 44.01/12.011 ~ 3.664; electric power allocation is a weighted redistribution; final output table structure should mirror Annex Tables A-5 through A-17


Corresponding script
R/08_co2_emissions.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions



This is a Tier 2 bottom-up methodology using EIA aggregate fuel consumption as its foundation. Key assumptions include: 100% oxidation of carbon during combustion; HHV (not LHV) energy basis throughout; use of No. 2 distillate as representative of all distillate grades; and U.S.-specific carbon content coefficients that vary annually for several fuel types.

Open question: EV electricity reallocation methodology (Browning 2018) – confirm the current implementation aligns with the most recent technical memo.
Open question: IPPU adjustment quantities (Step 2) need to be sourced consistently from the same IPPU module outputs to ensure cross-chapter consistency.
Open question: Confirm treatment of geothermal in Step 7 – binary/flash hybrids may require special handling.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.1 4.1 Cement Production
Overview. CO2 emissions from cement production arise from the calcination of calcium carbonate (limestone) during clinker production. The methodology applies a Tier 2 approach: national clinker production data are multiplied by a fixed emission factor (0.510 metric tons CO2 per metric ton clinker), with a 2% correction factor applied to account for cement kiln dust (CKD) not returned to the kiln. Data source transitions from USGS (1990-2013) to GHGRP (2014-2022).


2.1.1 Step 1 – Obtain clinker production data
National clinker production (metric tons) is compiled. For 1990-2013, data come from USGS mineral commodity surveys. From 2014 onward, GHGRP Subpart H facility-level reports are aggregated to a national total. An overlap comparison is performed to check consistency between the two sources at the transition year.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
USGS clinker production data (1990-2013); EPA GHGRP Subpart H (2014-2022)


Outputs
Annual clinker production time series (metric tons), 1990-2022


Key operations
Aggregate GHGRP facility-level data to national; splice USGS and GHGRP series at 2013/2014; overlap check


R notes
GHGRP data likely imported from CSV/API; dplyr::summarise() for national rollup; splice with bind_rows() after filtering by year range


Corresponding script
R/cement/01_clinker_production.R








2.1.2 Step 2 – Apply clinker emission factor and CKD correction
Clinker production is multiplied by the IPCC Tier 2 emission factor of 0.510 metric tons CO2 per metric ton clinker. A CKD correction factor of 1.02 is then applied to account for CO2 emissions from calcinated CKD that is not returned to the kiln.
Emissions = clinker production x 0.510 x 1.02






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Clinker production time series (Step 1); fixed emission factor = 0.510 t CO2/t clinker; CKD correction factor = 1.02


Outputs
Annual CO2 emissions from cement production (MMT CO2 Eq.)


Key operations
Multiply production x EF x CKD correction; unit conversion to MMT


R notes
Both factors are constants – store in a params list or header section for transparency; one-liner mutate


Corresponding script
R/cement/02_emissions_calculation.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions



This is a straightforward Tier 2 calculation with two fixed parameters. The main sources of uncertainty are the assumed 65% lime fraction in clinker and the default CKD correction factor.

Open question: Confirm that the GHGRP Subpart H data used does not include fuel combustion CO2 (only process CO2); some facilities report combined totals via CEMS.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.2 4.2 Lime Production
Overview. CO2 emissions from lime production result from the calcination of calcium and magnesium carbonates. The Tier 2 methodology multiplies high-calcium and dolomitic lime production separately by their respective stoichiometric emission factors, derived from the CaO and MgO content of lime (assumed 95% for both types).


2.2.1 Step 1 – Obtain lime production data by type
Annual production of high-calcium lime and dolomitic lime (metric tons) is obtained from USGS mineral commodity data for 1990-2021, and from GHGRP Subpart S for more recent years where applicable.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
USGS lime production by type; GHGRP Subpart S facility data (where used)


Outputs
Annual production of high-calcium and dolomitic lime (metric tons) by year


Key operations
Separate production into high-calcium vs. dolomitic categories; aggregate to national


R notes
Two-row output per year (one per lime type); or wide format with two columns


Corresponding script
R/lime/01_lime_production.R








2.2.2 Step 2 – Apply type-specific emission factors
Each lime type is multiplied by its stoichiometric emission factor:

High-calcium lime: EF = 0.95 x (44.01/56.08) = 0.7454 metric tons CO2/metric ton lime
Dolomitic lime: EF = 0.95 x [(44.01/56.08) + (44.01/84.31)] x 0.5 ~ 0.8364 metric tons CO2/metric ton lime

Total emissions are the sum across lime types.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Lime production by type (Step 1); type-specific emission factors (derived from stoichiometry)


Outputs
CO2 emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.) by lime type and total


Key operations
Multiply production x EF by lime type; sum to total


R notes
Emission factors are constants derived from molecular weights – document derivation clearly; group_by(lime_type) then summarise()


Corresponding script
R/lime/02_emissions_calculation.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions




Open question: Confirm current data source for lime production – USGS coverage vs. GHGRP Subpart S and transition year if applicable.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.3 4.3 Glass Production
Overview. CO2 emissions from glass production arise from the calcination of carbonate inputs (limestone, dolomite, soda ash, and other carbonates). A Tier 3 approach is used: quantities of each carbonate input are multiplied by carbonate-specific emission factors and mass fractions. For 2010-2022, GHGRP data provide carbonate input quantities; USGS data on soda ash supplement this. Pre-2010 data use a different source blend.


2.3.1 Step 1 – Obtain carbonate input quantities by type
For 2010-2022: quantities of limestone, dolomite, soda ash, barium carbonate, potassium carbonate, lithium carbonate, and strontium carbonate used in glass production are obtained from GHGRP and USGS. For earlier years, alternative data sources are used.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
GHGRP facility-level carbonate inputs (2010-2022); USGS soda ash consumption for glass; pre-2010 sources


Outputs
Annual carbonate input quantities (metric tons) by carbonate type


Key operations
Aggregate GHGRP facility data by carbonate type; supplement with USGS soda ash; handle pre-2010 differently


R notes
Year-conditional data sourcing – consider using a targets pipeline with separate data ingestion targets per source/period


Corresponding script
R/glass/01_carbonate_inputs.R








2.3.2 Step 2 – Apply carbonate-specific emission factors
Each carbonate is multiplied by its stoichiometric CO2 emission factor (metric tons CO2 per metric ton carbonate) and its average mineral mass fraction. Total emissions are summed across all carbonate types.
Emissions = Sum (carbonate quantity x emission factor x mass fraction)






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Carbonate quantities by type (Step 1); IPCC-derived emission factors and mass fractions by carbonate type


Outputs
CO2 emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.) from glass production


Key operations
Join carbonate quantities to EF lookup; multiply and sum


R notes
EF lookup table keyed on carbonate type; left_join() then mutate() and summarise()


Corresponding script
R/glass/02_emissions_calculation.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions




Open question: Clarify which specific carbonate types are covered by GHGRP Subpart H (glass) versus those requiring USGS supplementation. Confirm whether “other carbonates” in GHGRP align with the Inventory categorisation.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.4 4.4 Other Process Uses of Carbonates
Overview. This category covers CO2 emissions from limestone and dolomite consumed in non-glass, non-cement applications – flux stone, flue gas desulfurization (FGD), chemical stone, mine dusting, acid water treatment, and acid neutralization. It also covers soda ash consumption not associated with glass manufacturing. A Tier 2 approach is used for limestone and dolomite; a separate approach is used for soda ash.


2.4.1 Step 1 – Obtain limestone and dolomite consumption by end use
Annual consumption quantities (metric tons) of limestone and dolomite for each applicable end use are obtained from USGS.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
USGS mineral commodity data: limestone and dolomite consumption by end use


Outputs
Annual consumption by carbonate type and end use


Key operations
Filter to applicable end uses; aggregate if needed


R notes
Straightforward read and filter


Corresponding script
R/carbonates/01_consumption_data.R








2.4.2 Step 2 – Apply emission factors for limestone and dolomite
Fixed stoichiometric emission factors are applied:

Limestone: 0.43971 metric tons CO2 per metric ton carbonate
Dolomite: 0.47732 metric tons CO2 per metric ton carbonate







Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Consumption by type (Step 1); fixed emission factors


Outputs
CO2 emissions from limestone and dolomite consumption


Key operations
Multiply consumption x EF by carbonate type; sum


R notes
Constants stored in params; one mutate + summarise


Corresponding script
R/carbonates/02_limestone_dolomite_emissions.R








2.4.3 Step 3 – Estimate emissions from soda ash consumption
Soda ash consumption for non-glass uses is obtained from USGS. A soda ash-specific emission factor is applied, derived from the stoichiometry of Na2CO3 decomposition (consistent with IPCC 2006 Section 2.4.2.1).






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 3










Item
Detail




Inputs
USGS soda ash consumption (non-glass); stoichiometric emission factor for Na2CO3


Outputs
CO2 emissions from soda ash consumption


Key operations
Multiply consumption x EF


R notes
Can be combined with limestone/dolomite output in a single emissions table


Corresponding script
R/carbonates/03_soda_ash_emissions.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions




Open question: Confirm whether flux stone used in iron and steel production is excluded here (should be captured under 4.18) to avoid double-counting.

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.5 4.5 Ammonia Production
Overview. CO2 emissions from ammonia production arise from the use of natural gas or petroleum coke as a feedstock (hydrogen source) in steam methane reforming. For 2010-2022, a Tier 3 approach uses process CO2 emissions reported directly to GHGRP Subpart G. For 1990-2009, a Tier 2 approach uses feedstock consumption data multiplied by emission factors.


2.5.1 Step 1 – Obtain process CO2 data (2010-2022)
Facility-level CO2 emissions from ammonia production are obtained from GHGRP Subpart G and aggregated to a national annual total.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
GHGRP Subpart G facility reports (2010-2022)


Outputs
National CO2 emissions from ammonia production, 2010-2022


Key operations
Aggregate facility-level emissions to national total


R notes
dplyr::summarise() on GHGRP data filtered to Subpart G and ammonia production


Corresponding script
R/ammonia/01_ghgrp_emissions.R








2.5.2 Step 2 – Estimate emissions from feedstock data (1990-2009)
For years prior to GHGRP, feedstock consumption (natural gas and petroleum coke) used for ammonia production is obtained from EIA and other sources. Emissions are estimated by multiplying feedstock quantities by their carbon content coefficients (consistent with Tier 2 mass balance).






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
EIA natural gas and petroleum coke feedstock data for ammonia plants (1990-2009); carbon content coefficients from Annex 2.2


Outputs
CO2 emissions from ammonia production, 1990-2009


Key operations
Feedstock consumption x carbon content coefficient; convert to CO2


R notes
Share carbon content coefficients with the Energy chapter module for consistency


Corresponding script
R/ammonia/02_pre2010_emissions.R








2.5.3 Step 3 – Splice time series
The pre-2010 (Tier 2) and post-2010 (Tier 3/GHGRP) estimates are combined into a single consistent time series.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 3










Item
Detail




Inputs
Outputs from Steps 1 and 2


Outputs
Complete 1990-2022 CO2 emissions time series for ammonia production


Key operations
bind_rows() with year filter to avoid overlap; overlap-year comparison for QC


Corresponding script
R/ammonia/03_splice_time_series.R












Warning[NOTE] Summary and open questions




Open question: Feedstock CO2 from ammonia production is excluded from the Energy chapter (Step 2 of Annex 2.1). Confirm the exact adjustment amounts reconcile with the IPPU estimate for consistency.

text:
2.6 4.6 Urea Consumption for Non-Agricultural Purposes
Overview. When urea is applied or used industrially (non-fertiliser), the CO2 incorporated during its synthesis is released. Emissions are estimated by multiplying non-agricultural urea consumption by a stoichiometric factor (44/60), representing the mass of CO2 relative to urea (CH4N2O, MW = 60; CO2, MW = 44).


2.6.1 Step 1 – Obtain non-agricultural urea consumption
Annual urea consumption for non-agricultural purposes (metric tons) is obtained from industry sources and USGS.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
Non-agricultural urea consumption data (USGS or industry)


Outputs
Annual non-agricultural urea consumption (metric tons)


Corresponding script
R/urea/01_consumption.R








2.6.2 Step 2 – Apply stoichiometric emission factor
Emissions = urea consumption x (44/60)






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Non-agricultural urea consumption (Step 1)


Outputs
CO2 emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.) from urea use


Key operations
Multiply consumption x 44/60; unit conversion to MMT


R notes
Single constant factor; straightforward mutate


Corresponding script
R/urea/02_emissions_calculation.R

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.7 4.7 Nitric Acid Production
Overview. N2O is emitted as a byproduct during the catalytic oxidation of ammonia in nitric acid production. For 2010-2022, a Tier 3 approach uses N2O emissions and production data reported directly to GHGRP. For 1990-2009, a Tier 2 approach uses U.S. Census Bureau production data multiplied by IPCC default or abatement-adjusted emission factors.


2.7.1 Step 1 – Obtain N2O emissions and production data (2010-2022)
Facility-level N2O emissions and nitric acid production volumes are obtained from GHGRP and aggregated nationally. All U.S. facilities producing weak nitric acid (30-70%) are required to report.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1










Item
Detail




Inputs
GHGRP Subpart V facility-level N2O emissions and nitric acid production (2010-2022)


Outputs
National N2O emissions and production, 2010-2022


Key operations
Aggregate facility reports to national total


Corresponding script
R/nitric_acid/01_ghgrp_data.R








2.7.2 Step 2 – Estimate emissions from production data (1990-2009)
Nitric acid production from U.S. Census Bureau data is multiplied by Tier 2 emission factors, accounting for installed abatement technology where applicable.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
U.S. Census Bureau nitric acid production (1990-2009); IPCC default EFs; abatement technology assumptions


Outputs
N2O emissions, 1990-2009


Key operations
Production x EF; adjust for abatement where applicable


Corresponding script
R/nitric_acid/02_pre2010_emissions.R








2.7.3 Step 3 – Splice and express as CO2 equivalents
The two time series are combined and N2O emissions are converted to CO2 equivalents using the applicable GWP.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 3










Item
Detail




Key operations
bind_rows(); multiply N2O (metric tons) x GWP to get MMT CO2 Eq.


R notes
GWP value should be stored as a named constant consistent with the GWP set used across all Inventory categories


Corresponding script
R/nitric_acid/03_splice_and_gwp.R

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.8 4.8 Adipic Acid Production
Overview. N2O is produced as a byproduct of the catalytic oxidation of cyclohexane or cyclohexanone/cyclohexanol during adipic acid production. The Tier 2 methodology uses production data with IPCC default emission factors, adjusted for abatement where applicable. GHGRP data are used where available.


2.8.1 Step 1 – Obtain adipic acid production data
Annual adipic acid production (metric tons) is obtained from U.S. Census Bureau and/or GHGRP data.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1






Item
Detail




Inputs
U.S. Census Bureau or GHGRP production data


Outputs
Annual adipic acid production (metric tons)


Corresponding script
R/adipic_acid/01_production.R








2.8.2 Step 2 – Apply emission factor with abatement adjustment
Unadjusted N2O emissions are estimated using a default emission factor. Where abatement systems (catalytic decomposition or thermal oxidation) are installed, an abatement-adjusted effective emission factor is applied.
Emissions = production x EF x (1 - abatement efficiency x abatement fraction)






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Production (Step 1); IPCC default EF; plant-level abatement data


Outputs
N2O emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.) from adipic acid production


Key operations
EF x production; abatement adjustment where applicable; GWP conversion


Corresponding script
R/adipic_acid/02_emissions_calculation.R

section: 2.9 4.9 Caprolactam, Glyoxal and Glyoxylic Acid Production
text:
2.9 4.9 Caprolactam, Glyoxal and Glyoxylic Acid Production
Overview. N2O is generated during the high-temperature catalytic oxidation of ammonia in caprolactam production. Emissions are calculated using the IPCC Tier 1 method: caprolactam production is multiplied by a default emission factor. Glyoxal and glyoxylic acid are minor contributors also covered under this section.


2.9.1 Step 1 – Obtain production data
Annual caprolactam, glyoxal, and glyoxylic acid production (metric tons) from U.S. Census Bureau.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1






Item
Detail




Inputs
U.S. Census Bureau production data


Outputs
Annual production by chemical


Corresponding script
R/caprolactam/01_production.R








2.9.2 Step 2 – Apply Tier 1 emission factors
N2O emissions = production x default EF (IPCC 2006 Equation 3.9). Convert to CO2 equivalents using GWP.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
Production by chemical; IPCC Tier 1 EFs


Outputs
N2O emissions (MMT CO2 Eq.)


Key operations
Production x EF x GWP; sum across chemicals


Corresponding script
R/caprolactam/02_emissions_calculation.R

title: Inventory Methods Compilation
text:
2.10 4.10 Carbide Production and Consumption
Overview. CO2 and CH4 are emitted during the production of silicon carbide (SiC). CO2 is also emitted from consumption of SiC as a reducing agent. Production emissions use IPCC Tier 1 default factors. Consumption emissions use a country-specific stoichiometric approach (no IPCC guidance exists for SiC consumption).


2.10.1 Step 1 – Apply Tier 1 emission factors to SiC production
Annual SiC production (metric tons) x IPCC default EFs:

CO2: 2.62 metric tons CO2 per metric ton SiC
CH4: IPCC default CH4 factor







Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 1






Item
Detail




Inputs
U.S. Census Bureau SiC production; IPCC default EFs


Outputs
CO2 and CH4 emissions from SiC production


Corresponding script
R/carbide/01_production_emissions.R








2.10.2 Step 2 – Estimate CO2 from SiC consumption
SiC consumption data (metric tons) are multiplied by a stoichiometric emission factor derived from the chemistry of SiC use as a reducing agent.






Tip[CODING] Coding annotation – Step 2










Item
Detail




Inputs
SiC consumption data; country-specific stoichiometric EF


Outputs
CO2 emissions from SiC consumption


Corresponding script

2.18 4.18 Iron and Steel Production
Overview. CO2 is emitted from iron and steel production through: (1) metallurgical coke production, (2) pig iron production in blast furnaces, (3) basic oxygen furnace (BOF) steel production, (4) electric arc furnace (EAF) steel production, and (5) sinter and pellet production. All processes use a country-specific Tier 2 carbon mass balance approach. Carbonaceous inputs (coke, coal, limestone, electrodes, etc.) are tracked; non-CO2 carbon outputs (pig iron, steel, CO in off-gases) are subtracted.


2.18.1 Step 1 – Compile carbonaceous input and output data

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Architectural premise
Three layers, each keyed differently, connected by explicit link tables rather than by nesting:








Layer
Keyed by
Count (2026-11-13)




Retrieval
dataset_id
109 datasets


Computation
category
91 nodes in the category tree


Outputs
report, table, or Common Reporting Table (CRT) row
varies



The crosswalk between retrieval and computation is many-to-many: 278 links, connecting 87 of the 109 datasets to categories, or about 3.2 categories per linked dataset. The other 22 datasets are not yet linked to any category. Counts come from schema/parquet/. Retrieval therefore cannot live inside a category slice. Datasets are shared across categories, and duplicating ingestion per category guarantees drift between copies. The project rule is that every dataset has exactly one copy, whose home is derived from the crosswalk by dataset_home().
The unit of completable work is the vertical slice: one category’s computation, its methodology narrative, and its outputs, sitting on top of shared, horizontal retrieval and reference infrastructure.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 0: Foundations
These block everything downstream. Errors here propagate everywhere.

1. [x] Canonical units layer Canonical unit registry and conversion at ingestion (to_canonical() and canonical_units in {syrinx}); all downstream calculation unitless; conversion only at output. Blocks: all ingestion.
2. [~] Reference and vocabulary store CRT codes, gas list, global warming potential (GWP) sets (AR5 and successors), and the category hierarchy. The hub schema now has five tables (categories, datasets, the category-to-dataset crosswalk, the dictionary registry, and the drift log), edited as CSV files, built to Parquet by R/build_schema_parquet.R, and validated against schema/data-dict.yaml. Still to do: add gases and GWP sets, and make the store a versioned, pinned artifact rather than files in the repository. Blocks: computation, outputs, quality assurance.
3. [~] Methodology Narrative Standard Rules governing dataset citation, unit-handling discipline, uncertainty declaration, and dimensioned constants. A first written draft, version 0.1, is at Methodology Narrative Standard and awaits review. It leaves five questions open, including how to record emissions computed in one category but reported under another, and how to declare uncertainty (which waits on item 5). Blocks: every narrative, and therefore every category.
4. [~] Dataset dictionaries Target schema declared for each dataset, as data-dict.yaml files written against the tidyverse data-dict specification (version 0.1.0) and validated with the data-dict command-line tool, pinned to v0.0.3 and installed as a prebuilt binary. Each file describes a group of related tables: columns, types, constraints, relationships, and allowed values. The format is proven on the hub schema. No dataset dictionaries exist yet (0 of 109). Decisions made:

Grouping. One dictionary per group of related tables: one for the hub schema, one per source-category repository, and one for shared data.
Scope. Dictionaries describe cleaned Parquet files only, never raw downloads.
Link to retrieval. Each dataset’s dict_id in schema/ghgi_datasets.csv names its dictionary, and schema/ghgi_dictionaries.csv registers each dictionary’s path and status. Ingestion provenance stays in each dataset’s _metadata.yml, so the two do not declare the same facts. Pilot questions, answered on the hub schema:
Dictionaries are drafted from the cleaned table with the r-data-dict-builder custom AI tool, then reviewed by hand against the real data.
A failed check makes the tool exit with status 1, so a script or build can stop automatically. R/build_schema_parquet.R already does this.
Relationships cannot span dictionary files. Checks that a key exists in another repository’s data stay in R. Still open: the vocabularies for format, auth, update_frequency, and source_status are the observed values and need confirmation; 11 datasets fetched by API or scraping have no endpoint, so the schema build fails until they are filled in. Blocked by: 1, 2. Blocks: all ingestion. A sector pilot (probably waste) should finish before bulk ingestion begins.

5. [ ] Uncertainty parameter convention How a probability distribution is declared and attached to an input or a constant. Convention only, not the engine. Whether it relies on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) published uncertainty ranges or on propagated distributions is part of the decision. Blocked by: 1. Blocks: ingestion (see Trap 1).

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 1: Retrieval (keyed by dataset)
Retrieval flow, applied to every dataset:

Pull the data from the source, programmatically wherever possible.
Write the untouched result to the raw pin (item 8) before any cleaning.
Clean, harmonize, and standardize the data programmatically, converting to canonical units (item 1) and attaching any uncertainty parameters (item 5).
Write the cleaned table to Parquet in a disposable staging folder that also holds the relevant data-dict.yaml (item 4).
Validate against the data dictionary. This is a gate: if validation fails, nothing is written to the cleaned pin.
Write the validated data to the cleaned pin, with provenance metadata (item 8).
Downstream computation reads only from the cleaned pins.

The staging folder is rebuilt on every run and is never a permanent record; the pins board is the only permanent store.
Each dataset has two pins, {pin_stem}_raw and {pin_stem}_cleaned. Cleaned data keeps the source’s shape, with names, types, units, and layout standardized. Reshaping it into the intermediate table a category’s calculations expect (its canonical table) is a computation step, not a retrieval step; see item 12.

6. [~] Ingestion scripts and paired metadata (×109) Paired _ingest.R and _metadata.yml per dataset, carrying out steps 1 to 4 and 6 of the retrieval flow and emitting canonicalized Parquet. The _metadata.yml records the dataset’s source and retrieval details. Blocked by: 4, 5.
7. [~] Validation (×109) The division of labor is settled: the data-dict tool owns structural checks (types, required values, keys, links between tables in one dictionary, allowed values, and row-level assertions); {pointblank} owns quality thresholds at ingestion and output; checks against another repository’s data stay in R; {testthat} covers calculation functions. Blocked by: 4. Develop alongside 6.
8. [~] Pins boards and raw-vintage capture Two kinds of pin per dataset:

Raw pin: an immutable, dated snapshot of source data exactly as retrieved. If a cleaning rule changes later, the cleaning can be rerun from this pin without downloading again, and the original source content can be shown.
Cleaned pin: the validated, canonicalized output, written only after the dictionary gate passes. Every pin write carries provenance metadata: the source address, the retrieval date, and the version of the cleaning code. Pin names derive from each dataset’s pin_stem. The board is derived by dataset_home(): a dataset used by one sector lives on that sector’s board, and the 7 datasets used by two or more sectors live in a shared-data repository. Still open: where the shared board is hosted, and whether raw and cleaned pins share a board. Blocked by: nothing for the raw pin. Do early: this data is unrecoverable if not captured at retrieval time. Writes to the cleaned pin are gated by items 4 and 7.

9. [ ] Prior-published-vintage store Every prior published release, held as a queryable input dataset rather than as an archive. Blocked by: 2. Blocks: recalculation.
10. [x] Constants store Emission factors, GWPs, and dimensionless parameters, each declaring its native unit basis and canonicalized at ingestion. Extend to carry distributions per item 5.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 2: Computation (keyed by category)

11. [~] Methodology narrative per category (×91) The authoritative specification. Precise about inputs, outputs, transformations, and decision rules; implementation-agnostic. Written to the standard (item 3), one per category, named by node_id. The wastewater example is the only one so far. The Inventory Methods Compilation is source material for writing them, not a specification. Blocked by: 3.
12. [~] Computation pipeline per category (×91) Reads inputs only from cleaned pins. Each pipeline first maps its cleaned inputs onto the category’s canonical intermediate table, which has its own dictionary (the canonical tier in schema/ghgi_dictionaries.csv, linked by canonical_dict_id in the category table). Canonical tables belong to the category, not to a dataset, because one dataset feeds about three categories. They can be pinned per category later if that proves useful. The convention is pending the Fossil Fuel Combustion pilot. Blocked by: 6, 10, 11.
13. [ ] Splice and time-series-consistency operations Documented, coded, reusable methods for overlap, surrogate, interpolation, and extrapolation. A first-class operation, not a patch applied when a source is discontinued. Blocked by: 6. Needed now for at least one discontinued source.
14. [ ] Emissions store schema The canonical long-format result table that all categories write into. This is the freeze point (see Trap 2). It should also have a data dictionary (item 4), so results are validated by the same mechanism as inputs. Blocked by: 2. Blocks: 15 to 20.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 3: Cross-cutting analytics
These read the whole emissions store. None of them fit inside a per-category slice.

15. [ ] Quality assurance reconciliation Category totals, then CRT rollups, then the national total; cross-category consistency checks. Blocked by: 14.
16. [ ] Uncertainty propagation engine Monte Carlo simulation over the computation graph, returning quantiles. Distinct from the parameters (item 5), which are a domain-expert product. Blocked by: 5, 14.
17. [ ] Key category analysis Approach 1 and Approach 2 (the latter requires 16). Blocked by: 14, 16.
18. [ ] Recalculation and vintage comparison Current versus prior published estimates for the same historical year, with each difference attributed to its cause. This is an annual reporting obligation, not an optional analysis. Blocked by: 9, 14.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 4: Outputs

19. [ ] Figure and table suite Standard figures and tables against a fixed style guide. Blocked by: 14.
20. [~] Inventory database and CRT export Terminal output block; final unit conversion (for example, gigagrams to teragrams) occurs only at this step. Blocked by: 14, 15.
21. [~] Quarto report and website Site configuration and publishing through continuous integration. Whether and where to publish is not yet decided. Blocked by: 19; content blocked by 11.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Tier 5: Governance
Runs alongside the build, not after it.

22. [~] Drift detection as a build target Automated comparison of narrative and code that fails the build rather than silently reconciling. A difference is a meaningful signal, not a contradiction to suppress. The drift log table (validation_log) is defined in the hub schema but empty. A failed dictionary validation already stops the hub schema build, since the tool exits with an error status. Blocked by: 3, 12.
23. [ ] Release definition A precise answer to “what object is the annual submission”: hashed, immutable, pinned, and reproducible from a dependency lockfile plus the raw vintage. The release should record the dictionary files and the data-dict tool version, so it can be re-validated exactly as it was. Blocked by: 8, 14.
24. [x] Custom AI tool chain Narrative to structured framework to code to plain-language documentation, plus the data-dictionary builder. Must track versions of the Narrative Standard and of AGENTS.md. Blocked by: 3.
25. [~] Repository and continuous integration infrastructure Dependency pinning, pipeline orchestration, continuous integration, and coordination across repositories. The data-dict tool is a standalone binary, so renv.lock does not record it; its version is pinned in AGENTS.md, and continuous integration must download that exact release. renv.lock also does not yet record {arrow} and {here}. A GitHub Actions workflow for the schema build is planned.

title: Component Build Checklist
text:
Ordering traps
Trap 1: Uncertainty reaches backward into ingestion. Item 5 sits in Tier 0 deliberately. The propagation engine (16) may be years away, but the convention for declaring distributions must exist before ingestion is written. Ingesting 109 datasets with no place to attach a distribution means reopening 109 ingestion scripts later.
Trap 2: The schema freeze (item 14) is earlier than it feels. Everything in Tiers 3 and 4 blocks on the emissions store schema. The instinct is to defer it until enough categories exist to “see the shape.” Resist this: the schema is derivable from CRT and inventory-database output requirements, which are already fixed and externally specified.
Trap 3: The dictionary tool is pre-1.0, and every ingestion script depends on it. The data-dict tool is at v0.0.3, so its behavior may change between releases. The hub schema pilot settled the main questions (how failure is reported, whether relationships can span files), but it covered metadata tables, not sector data. Run the sector pilot before writing ingestion in bulk, and check each new release before upgrading the pinned version.
A note on quality assurance. Quality assurance is not a module. It is a property of every boundary: data-contract validation at ingestion, unit tests on functions, reconciliation at output. It appears in this list only where it takes the form of a discrete deliverable.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
What this category covers
This category covers methane and nitrous oxide from the treatment and discharge of domestic and industrial wastewater. It is organized into two subsources:

Domestic wastewater — from residential and commercial sources, treated at publicly owned treatment works (POTWs) or in septic systems, plus emissions from treated effluent discharged to receiving waters.
Industrial wastewater — from industries that generate high-organic-load wastewater treated on site, covering breweries, ethanol production, pulp and paper, meat and poultry, petroleum refining, and fruit and vegetable processing.

It does not cover: biogenic carbon dioxide from wastewater (excluded from national totals by convention); methane recovered and combusted for energy, which is netted out of this category’s emissions (see step-by-step); or emissions from biosolids once they leave the treatment system (see connections).

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
section: Emission factors and other fixed values
text:
Emission factors and other fixed values

Methane emission factors by treatment pathway and by industry — methane produced per unit of organic load (e.g., kg CH₄ per kg BOD or COD). [placeholder]. Source: [reference].
Nitrous oxide emission factors for effluent and for applicable industries — N₂O per unit of nitrogen load. [placeholder]. Source: [reference].
Organic load factors — BOD or COD generated per person (domestic) or per unit of production (industrial). [placeholder]. Source: [reference].
Methane correction factors for each treatment pathway (the degree to which conditions are anaerobic). [placeholder]. Source: [reference].
Global warming potentials (AR5) for CH₄ and N₂O, used to express results as CO₂-equivalent.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Units

Inputs arrive in mixed units: population in persons, production in industry-specific units (for example barrels and tons), wastewater flows in volume units, and protein in mass per person per day.
Results are reported in gigagrams of CH₄ and N₂O, and in carbon dioxide equivalent for summary tables.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Connections to other categories

Upstream: none. All inputs are datasets, not other categories’ results.
Downstream: category totals feed the Waste sector and national CH₄ and N₂O totals.
Attribution:

Anaerobic digesters at water resource recovery facilities, and digestion of wastewater sludge, are reported here in 5D, not under Anaerobic Digestion (5B2). See the anaerobic digester and sludge digestion rules in Cross-Sector Boundary Rules.
Sewage sludge incineration is assessed as insignificant and not estimated (waste incineration rule).
Biosolids sent to landfills or applied to land are accounted for in those categories. No boundary rule covers this yet; one should be added to the boundary rules.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
section: How the calculation works, step by step
text:
How the calculation works, step by step

Configure the model constants from the constants source.
Domestic — organic load: use population and domestic treatment data to estimate the volume of domestic wastewater and its organic (BOD) load, split across treatment pathways.
Domestic — tertiary flow: estimate the share of flow receiving tertiary treatment (constructed wetlands), fitted from historical data where direct figures are unavailable.
Domestic — CH₄: compute methane from domestic treatment and from discharged effluent, using the organic load, treatment-pathway fractions, methane correction factors, and emission factors.
Domestic — energy recovery: forecast anaerobic digester flow at POTWs, and subtract the methane recovered and combusted for energy from the domestic total.
Domestic — N₂O: compute nitrous oxide from effluent, deriving the nitrogen load from protein supply and consumption, then applying the effluent N₂O emission factor.
Industrial — by industry: for each industry (breweries, ethanol, pulp and paper, meat and poultry, petroleum refining, fruit and vegetable processing), estimate wastewater generation and organic load from production data, then compute CH₄ — and N₂O for industries where it applies — using the industry-specific emission factors. Subtract industrial energy recovery where methane is captured.
Aggregate: sum domestic and industrial CH₄ and N₂O.
Apply global warming potentials to express totals as CO₂-equivalent, and arrange the result for the inventory database.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Rules and judgment calls

Treatment-pathway fractions: the split of domestic wastewater across aerobic, anaerobic, and septic pathways is set by [rule]. The anaerobic fraction governs methane and is the most consequential. Decided by: [who].
Septic share held constant: the American Housing Survey share of households on septic systems is held constant over [years], because [reason].
Tertiary flow estimation: where direct constructed-wetland flow data are not available, the share is fitted from the historical trend rather than assumed constant.
Digester flow forecasting: for inventory years beyond the available digester data, flow is forecast by [method] rather than carried forward unchanged.
Which industries get N₂O: breweries, pulp and paper, meat and poultry, and petroleum refining are estimated for both CH₄ and N₂O. Ethanol and fruit and vegetable processing are estimated for CH₄ only, because [reason].
Load basis: domestic emissions are calculated on a BOD basis, and industrial emissions on [a BOD or COD] basis depending on the industry, per [rule].

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
section: Known changes and things to watch
text:
Known changes and things to watch

The protein consumption series feeding the domestic N₂O calculation changed source for GHGIA 2026, so years before and after the change are not directly comparable.
Digester flow data lag the inventory year, so recent years rely on the forecast in step 4 rather than reported flow.
Eight datasets used by this method are not yet in the dataset registry. They need registering, and the crosswalk updating, before this narrative can be approved.

title: GHGI Glossary
text: This glossary defines the terms and abbreviations used across the GHGI (Greenhouse Gas Inventory) pipeline.

title: GHGI Glossary
text:
Reporting and methodology
CRT (Common Reporting Tables). The standardized table format used to report national greenhouse gas inventories to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. Emissions intermediates in the code are named after CRT row letters, for example f1_ch4_emissions.
GWP (global warming potential). A factor that expresses how much a gas warms the atmosphere relative to carbon dioxide over a fixed period, used to convert emissions of different gases into carbon dioxide equivalents. This project uses the values from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5).
IPCC Tier 1 and Tier 2. Levels of methodological detail in IPCC guidance. Tier 1 uses default emission factors supplied by the IPCC. Tier 2 uses country-specific factors and more detailed activity data. Tier 3 is more detailed still.
GHGRP (Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program). The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency program under which large emitters report their emissions directly. Its data is one input to several source categories.
LMOP (Landfill Methane Outreach Program). An Environmental Protection Agency program that maintains a database of landfills and landfill gas energy projects.
FOD (first-order decay). A model in which waste decomposes, and produces methane, at a rate proportional to the amount of decomposable material remaining. It is used for landfill methane.
BOD and COD (biochemical and chemical oxygen demand). Measures of the organic content of wastewater, which drives methane production in wastewater treatment.
MOVES (Motor Vehicle Emission Simulator). The Environmental Protection Agency’s model of emissions from on-road vehicles. The code currently uses MOVES3, while the GHGIA 2026 report refers to MOVES5. This is a known difference between code and narrative.
FFC (fossil fuel combustion). The largest Energy source category (CRT 1A): carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide from burning coal, natural gas, and petroleum for energy.
FOKS (Fuel Oil and Kerosene Sales). An Energy Information Administration (EIA) survey of distillate and residual fuel oil and kerosene sales by end use. Discontinued in 2020.
Gg and Tg (gigagram and teragram). Units of mass. One teragram equals one thousand gigagrams. Inputs are handled in gigagrams, and the conversion to teragrams happens only at the final output step.
MMT CO2 Eq. (million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent). The unit used in EPA and GHGIA report tables. One million metric tons equals one teragram, so MMT CO2 Eq. and Tg CO2 Eq. are the same quantity.

title: GHGI Glossary
text:
Project practices
Spec-driven development (SDD). A way of building software in which a written specification, not the programmer’s judgment, defines what the code must do. Here, domain experts write the specifications as methodology narratives.
Canonical units. The single agreed unit for each kind of quantity. Every input is converted to its canonical unit at ingestion, and the canonical_units tibble in {syrinx} records them.
Drift. A disagreement between what the methodology narrative says and what the code does. The project treats drift as useful information to be reported, not as noise to be smoothed over.

title: GHGI Glossary
text:
Packages
{targets} and {tarchetypes}. Tools for defining the pipeline as a graph of steps that are re-run only when their inputs change.
{pins}. Versioned storage for datasets.
{pointblank}. Data validation checks.
{syrinx}. The project’s internal package for cleaning data and converting units to canonical units. It lives at joewcorra/syrinx.

This page shows AGENTS.md from the repository root. That file is the single source of truth for conventions and is also read by AI coding tools, so edit it there, not here.

title: Project Conventions
text:
What this project is
This repository is part of a spec-driven R pipeline for the U.S. Greenhouse Gas Inventory (GHGI). “Spec-driven” means that domain experts write plain-language methodology narratives, and those narratives define what the code must do. Code is written to follow a specification, never to guess at one. The goal is auditability and institutional resilience: the methods should be documented and reproducible even if any one person leaves.

title: Project Conventions
text:
How to work with me

I code exclusively in R. I also use HTML and CSS when a document or app needs them. Do not write Python.
Work incrementally. Prove a pattern on one source category before scaling it to others, and stop at human-review checkpoints instead of pushing ahead.
Fail loudly, not silently. If an input is missing, a unit is unrecognized, or a methodology step is ambiguous, raise an error or ask me. Do not guess or fill in a plausible value.
Keep the methodology specification and the code separate. If the code disagrees with the narrative (for example, code that uses an older model version than the narrative cites), report the difference to me. Do not quietly reconcile it, because the difference is useful information.
I will correct direction mid-conversation. Fold those corrections into everything that follows.
Write in full sentences. Spell out acronyms the first time they appear, and define technical terms briefly where they are introduced. Avoid symbolic shorthand in prose. Inside code and code comments, normal programming notation is fine.
Be concise by default, and expand when I ask.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Repository structure

ghgi-roadmap-and-crosscutting (this repository) is the coordination hub. It holds the schema registry, methodology narratives, cross-cutting design decisions, and this file. It does not pull, transform, or calculate emissions data.
Each sector has its own source-category repository: ghg-energy, ghg-ippu, ghg-agriculture, ghg-lulucf, and ghg-waste. Each one handles data pulling, transformation, aggregation, calculation, and visualization for its sector.
There is no shared ghg-core repository. The source-category hierarchy, the dataset registry, and their crosswalk live in this repository’s schema/ folder.
syrinx is the internal helper package (see Tools and packages).

Each source-category repository follows this layout:
ghg-[sector]/
├── README.md             Sector overview and quick start
├── METHODOLOGY.md        Methodology documentation
├── data/
│   ├── reference/        Emission factors and lookup tables
│   ├── activity/         Processed activity data
│   └── calculated/       Results, date-stamped
├── data-raw/             Original downloads (git-ignored)
├── R/
│   ├── 01_download.R     Data acquisition
│   ├── 02_clean.R        Cleaning and harmonization
│   ├── 03_calculate.R    Emission calculations
│   ├── 04_validate.R     Quality assurance and quality control checks

title: Project Conventions
text:
R coding conventions

Functions and naming

Name data-retrieval functions get_[scope]_[source]_[gas](). This applies to emissions data retrieval only; schema and metadata functions (for example, loading or validating the category/dataset registry) are named descriptively instead, such as read_ghgi_schema() and dataset_home().
Function names describe the output, not the process: get_, not calculate_.
Name intermediate emissions objects with the Common Reporting Table (CRT) row letter, for example f1_ch4_emissions.
Write one function per logical calculation phase. Each function takes named data-frame arguments plus, where needed, a named constants vector, and returns a single tibble with an explicit return(). The one exception is a category-level function, which returns a list (see Organizing a category).
Functions have no side effects: they do not write files, print, or modify global state.
Helpers shared between national-level and state-level compilation live in a common script. Helpers specific to one level stay in that level’s script. Name helpers descriptively in snake_case; an h_ prefix is optional and only distinguishes a helper from a get_ function.



Organizing a category

Organize each category as a named list built with tibble::lst(), holding one tibble per subcategory. For example, electric power generation holds gas_combustion, coal_combustion, and so on.
Compute each subcategory in its own function, so the code for one subcategory is easy to find, debug, and change without touching the others.
The category-level function returns the list with an explicit return():

get_[scope]_[category] <- function(...) {
  gas_combustion  <- get_[scope]_[gas_subcategory]_[gas](...)
  coal_combustion <- get_[scope]_[coal_subcategory]_[gas](...)
  return(lst(gas_combustion, coal_combustion))
}


Style

Use the magrittr pipe %>%, not the native pipe |>.
Use the tidyverse style. Avoid nested if/else. Prefer switch(), named-vector lookups, dplyr::case_when(), guard clauses with early returns, and match.arg(). Vectorized ifelse() and dplyr::if_else() are fine.
Give every case_when() a .default clause. Use if_else() for binary logic. When a branch depends on a value computed earlier in the same mutate(), split the work into sequential mutate() calls.
Iterate with {purrr} (map(), map_dfr(), map2(), walk()). Do not use for loops or the apply(), lapply(), and sapply() family.
Extract columns with pull(), not $.
Use snake_case for variable names. Character data is lowercase, with no punctuation except hyphens.



Data shape and columns

Keep time series in long format. Never pivot to wide format inside a calculation function.
Year columns are factors. Apply forcats::as_factor(year) whenever a year column is created, for example when scaffolding a series with tibble(year = start:end).
Do not put unit suffixes in column names (waste_composted, not waste_composted_kt). Unit context belongs in the data dictionary.
Name emission columns [gas]_emissions (for example co2_emissions) and carbon dioxide equivalent columns [gas]_co2e.



Joins, grouping, and output

Attach treatment tables with an inline left_join(), then filter(), then select().
Every join specifies by explicitly.
Follow every group_by() with summarize(..., .groups = "drop").
Build collated results with tibble() followed by pull().
End each script with a section headed ## Output, which holds the final output block.



Gap-filling and period splits
Fill gaps with lag() and lead() inside sequential mutate() calls. Handle methodology breaks between periods with case_when() on a year threshold:
mutate(value = if_else(
  is.na(value),
  lag(value, 1) + ((lead(value, 1) - lag(value, 1)) / 2),
  value))

mutate(value = case_when(
  year <= [threshold_year] ~ [method_a_expression],
  .default = [method_b_expression]))


Constants

Pass emission factors, global warming potentials, and other parameters as a single named numeric vector, and reference values by name (constants["c_content_rubber"]), never as bare numbers.
Unit conversions never live in the constants vector or inside a get_ function. See Unit discipline.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Unit discipline

Convert every input to the project’s canonical units at ingestion.
Keep all intermediate calculations unitless.
Convert units only at the final output step, using named constants (for example, gigagrams to teragrams).
Constants that carry units, such as emission factors, must declare their native unit basis and be converted to canonical units at ingestion.
Species-conversion ratios, such as 44 divided by 12 for carbon to carbon dioxide, do not change with scale. Treat them differently from emission factors, which do depend on scale.
{units} is an ingestion-layer tool only. It is never used inside a calculation function.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Architecture principles

The meta-module (the layer holding the narratives and the schema) is a control plane. It should produce and constrain the pipeline, not merely accompany it.
Two decisions must come early: the uncertainty convention must be settled before ingestion is built, and the emissions store schema should be frozen sooner than it feels necessary.
Data quality is enforced by validation checks at ingestion and at output.

The reasoning behind these principles is in explanation/architecture.qmd.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Tools and packages

Pipeline orchestration: {targets} and {tarchetypes} are optional for now; whether to adopt them is an open decision (see Open decisions in explanation/architecture.qmd). Write every calculation function so it could become a {targets} step without rewriting: inputs passed as arguments, no side effects, and one returned tibble (or, for a category-level function, one list of tibbles).
Versioned data storage: {pins}.
File formats: Parquet through {arrow}. Ingestion provenance goes in _metadata.yml.
Data dictionaries: one data-dict.yaml file per related group of tables, written against the tidyverse data-dict.yaml specification (version 0.1.0). Relationships cannot span files, so tables that join to each other share one dictionary: one for this repository’s schema (schema/data-dict.yaml), one per source-category repository, and one for shared data. Dictionaries describe cleaned Parquet files only, never raw downloads. Each column gets its type, constraints, and a range, examples, or values entry verified against the real data. Validate with the data-dict command-line tool, pinned to v0.0.3 (prebuilt binary from the tidyverse/data-dict GitHub releases), at all three levels: validate-spec, validate-meta, and validate-data. Record unfinished work in the dictionary’s todo keys rather than in comments.
Validation: the data-dict tool owns structural checks (types, required values, unique and primary keys, links between tables, allowed values, and row-level assertions). {pointblank} owns quality thresholds at ingestion and output. Checks that a key exists in another repository’s data stay in R. {testthat} covers unit tests of calculation functions.
Dataset placement: every dataset has exactly one copy. Where it lives is derived from the crosswalk, not entered by hand: a dataset used by one sector lives in that sector’s repository, and a dataset used by two or more sectors lives in a shared-data repository published through {pins}. dataset_home() in R/ghgi_schema.R computes it.
Internal helper package: {syrinx} (from joewcorra/syrinx). It provides pre_clean(), use_dictionary(), apply_metadata_labels(), to_canonical(), to_canonical_all(), and the canonical_units tibble. Use these instead of writing new cleaning or unit-conversion code. Call pre_clean() at the end of a function’s pipeline whenever its output will be passed downstream or stored. Install it as needed with remotes::install_github("joewcorra/syrinx"), adding auth_token = Sys.getenv("GITHUB_PAT") if the repository is private.
Data manipulation: the tidyverse ({dplyr}, {tidyr}, {purrr}, {readr}, {stringr}, {forcats}, {lubridate}, {tibble}), {janitor} (many of its functions are wrapped in {syrinx}), {labelled}, {readxl} and {openxlsx} for Excel files, {jsonlite}, {httr2} for APIs, {rvest} for scraping, {here} for paths, and {furrr} for parallel iteration.
Spatial data (mainly LULUCF): {sf}, {terra}, and {mapview}.
Reporting: {gt} (with {gtExtras}) for tables and {ggplot2} (with {patchwork}, {scales}, and {showtext}) for figures. {visNetwork} can diagram pipeline dependencies. Documentation is written in Quarto and rendered to HTML; diagrams use Mermaid. Whether and where to publish the documentation is not yet decided.
Documentation assistance through direct large language model API calls: {ellmer}.
Package reproducibility: {renv}. Each repository has its own renv.lock; run renv::restore() to reproduce it.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Custom AI tools

Custom skills for this project live in ~/.claude/skills/, outside this repository. Use them when they apply: ghg-methodology-parser, r-ghg-coder, r-methodology-narrator, and r-data-dict-builder.
The typical flow for one source category: the parser turns chapter text into an implementation framework, the coder turns the framework into an R script, and the narrator turns the script back into a plain-language narrative for review by the source lead. The data-dictionary builder runs independently against any table, most usefully once a function’s output is stable.
Each skill’s SKILL.md must agree with this file. When a convention changes, update this file first, then the affected SKILL.md.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Project management

Cross-cutting issues and the roadmap live in the ghgi-roadmap-and-crosscutting repository. Source-category repositories hold category-specific issues. Work across all repositories is tracked on the single GitHub Project board named “ghgi”.
Board columns: Backlog, Ready, In Progress, Review, Done, and Blocked.
Cross-repository issue labels: sector: (for example sector:energy), priority: (high, medium, low), type: (bug, feature, documentation), and status: (blocked, ready-for-review).
GitHub Actions run {testthat} on push.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Decision authority
Ask the owner of a decision rather than making it:

The data system developer decides R package choices, code organization, Git workflow details, and development tools.
Collaborative decisions: data storage and databases, major workflow changes, data access and sharing policies, and public-facing features.
Sector leads decide sector-specific methodology, data source selection, quality assurance and quality control thresholds, and reporting priorities.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Reference sources

The GHGIA Full Report 2026 (University of Maryland Center for Global Sustainability) is the canonical source for units and methodology.
Use the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) global warming potentials.
Secondary references: the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories for emission factor tiers and calculation approaches, the EPA inventory reports and annexes, and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change reporting requirements for the Common Reporting Tables.

title: Project Conventions
text:
Writing about this project

Avoid wording that implies criticism of colleagues or of earlier workflows. For example, say a legacy Excel process is “less efficient,” not “clunky.”
For general audiences, say “custom AI tools” rather than “Claude Skills,” and emphasize that the tools follow a human-designed specification.

title: Maintain the Schema
text: The schema is edited as CSV files, checked against a data dictionary by the data-dict command-line tool, and stored as Parquet. You edit two kinds of file; the rest are generated or only read. The table layouts are described in the schema reference.

title: Maintain the Schema
text:
Which files to touch



File
What you do with it




schema/*.csv
Edit. This is the content: categories, datasets, the crosswalk, the dictionary registry, and the drift log. Separate multiple values in one cell with semicolons (for example CO2;CH4). Leave a cell empty when there is no value; do not use a dash as a placeholder.


schema/data-dict.yaml
Edit only when the structure changes: a new column, a new allowed value, or a new rule. Record unfinished work as a todo: entry so the tool reports it on every run.


R/build_schema_parquet.R
Run after any edit. Do not edit unless a column is added or removed.


R/ghgi_schema.R
Use for queries; see Query the schema.


schema/parquet/
Generated by the build script. Never edit.


docs/
Generated by quarto render. Never edit; see Render the documents.


schema/schema-dictionary.html
Generated by the build script. Never edit. quarto render copies it into docs/schema/.

title: Maintain the Schema
text:
Build and validate
After editing any CSV file, run:
source(here::here("R", "build_schema_parquet.R"))
This rebuilds the Parquet files and validates them at three levels: the dictionary itself, the column names and types, and the values. If any check fails, the script stops and the message names the rule and the rows that broke it. Fix the CSV file, or the rule if the rule is wrong, and run it again. Warnings about unresolved todo entries are reminders, not failures.
When every check passes, the script also regenerates schema/schema-dictionary.html, a browsable page of the dictionary for colleagues who don’t use R or Git. It is a single file that opens in any browser, so copy it to the shared drive after each rebuild.
The script needs the data-dict command-line tool, version 0.0.3, either on your PATH or in ~/bin (C:\Users\<you>\bin on Windows). Install the prebuilt binary from the tidyverse/data-dict releases (on Windows, data-dict-cli-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip) and check it against its .sha256 file. Do not build it from source.

title: Maintain the Schema
text:
Adding a new dataset

Add a row to ghgi_datasets.csv, and link it to the categories that use it in ghgi_category_datasets.csv.
Run the build.
Run dataset_home(schema) to see where the dataset belongs: a sector’s name means that sector’s repository, and shared means the shared-data repository.
In that repository, once the cleaned table exists, add it to the repository’s data-dict.yaml. The r-data-dict-builder custom AI tool can draft the entry.
Validate that dictionary with data-dict validate-data <folder>.
Register the dictionary in ghgi_dictionaries.csv, set the dataset’s dict_id to it, and run the build again.
