title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text: Draft. This version collects rules that already exist in AGENTS.md, the schema, and the component build checklist, and the section structure of the wastewater example. Points marked [Open] have not been decided. They are listed together at the end.

title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text:
Purpose
A methodology narrative is the specification for one source category. It says, in plain language, what the category estimates, which data and constants it uses, and exactly how the estimate is calculated. The code is written to follow the narrative, never the other way round.
A narrative has three readers:

Domain reviewers and auditors, who check that the method is right without reading code.
Developers, who turn it into R code, with the help of the custom AI tools.
Future staff, who need to understand and reproduce the method if the author leaves.

A narrative is not a copy of the inventory chapter, and it contains no code. Where the Inventory Methods Compilation covers a category, use it as raw material; once the category’s narrative is approved, the narrative replaces that section. It may restate the chapter’s method, but it must be complete and precise enough that someone could implement the category from the narrative alone, in any language.

title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text:
Scope and files

Write one narrative per category that is calculated as a unit. A narrative may cover that category’s child sources and subsources, and must then list each one under Scope.
Name the file after the category’s node_id in the schema, for example wastewater_treatment.qmd.
[Open] Where narratives are stored: here in reference/methodology/, or in each sector’s repository as METHODOLOGY.md, which the standard repository layout also mentions.

title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text:
Required sections
Every narrative has these sections, with these headings, in this order. If a section does not apply, keep the heading and say why in one sentence.

1. Identification

Category name, as source_name in the schema.
node_id of the category and of every source it covers.
CRT code or codes. CRT means Common Reporting Table, the United Nations reporting format.
Sector, and the gases estimated.
Inventory edition, for example GHGIA 2026.
Author (the source lead), reviewer, and the date last revised.
The version of this standard the narrative follows.

The node_id, CRT code, and gases must match schema/ghgi_categories.csv. If they do not, report the difference so one of them can be corrected. Do not change the narrative to match quietly.


2. Scope
What the category covers, organized by source and subsource. Then what it does not cover, naming for each exclusion the category or rule that does cover it, or saying that it is not estimated and why.


3. Data sources
One entry per dataset. Each entry gives:

The dataset’s dataset_id from the dataset registry, for example DS-CENSUS-POP, and its name.
Its role, using the crosswalk’s values: activity_data, emission_factor, or parameter.
Whether the category can be estimated without it (the crosswalk’s required).
What it is used for, and the years it covers.

The list must agree with the crosswalk in schema/ghgi_category_datasets.csv. A dataset that is not yet in the registry is added to the registry first. Until then, list it with “[not registered]” in place of an ID.


4. Emission factors and other constants
One entry per constant. Each entry gives:

Its name, in snake_case. This is the name the code uses to look the value up, for example ef_clinker.
Its value, or values by year or by type.
Its native unit basis, for example metric tons of carbon dioxide per metric ton of clinker.
Its source, with table or page, and the years it applies to.

Rules:

The calculation steps refer to constants by name, never by bare number.
Use the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) global warming potentials, cited by reference rather than listed again.
Identify species-conversion ratios, such as 44/12 for carbon to carbon dioxide, as conversion ratios rather than emission factors. They do not depend on scale.



5. Units

The native units of each input as received.
The reporting unit of the results.

Every input is converted to the project’s canonical units at ingestion, and results are converted to reporting units only at the final output step. Steps therefore do not include unit conversions. If a conversion carries methodological meaning, such as a heating-value basis, describe it here.


6. Connections to other categories

Upstream: inputs this category takes from another category’s results.
Downstream: categories or totals that use this category’s results.
Attribution: emissions calculated here but reported under another category, or the reverse. Each case cites the matching rule in Cross-Sector Boundary Rules. If no rule exists, say so; that rule is added there, not settled in the narrative.
[Open] The detailed attribution rule (checklist item 3): how a narrative records an emission that is computed in one category and reported in another.



7. Calculation steps
A numbered list, in the order the calculation runs. Each step states:

What goes in: datasets by dataset_id, constants by name, or the results of earlier steps by step number.
What it does, in words, with a simple formula where it helps, for example “emissions equal clinker production × ef_clinker × ckd_correction”.
What comes out.

Rules:

One step is one logical phase of the calculation. A reader should be able to check each step on its own.
A change of method between periods names the threshold year and the method on each side, for example “1990 to 2013: method A; 2014 onward: method B”.
Gaps, splices between sources, and extrapolation to recent years each name the method used (for example linear interpolation, overlap, or surrogate), the years affected, and the reason.
Do not name R functions, packages, scripts, or columns. The narrative describes the method, not its code.



8. Rules and judgment calls
Every decision rule or assumption that is not dictated by the source data: what was decided, why, and who decided it, where known. Methodology decisions belong to the sector lead.


9. Uncertainty
[Open] Pending the uncertainty convention (checklist item 5). Until it is settled, list any published uncertainty range for each input or constant, with its source, or write “not yet declared”.


10. Known changes and things to watch
Changes from the previous edition, discontinued or at-risk sources, and recent years that rely on estimates rather than reported data. Link the Sector Data Notes rather than repeating them.


11. References
Cite the GHGIA 2026 chapter and section, the 2006 IPCC Guidelines (volume and chapter), and the EPA inventory annexes, as applicable.

title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text:
Writing rules

Write in full sentences. Spell out each acronym the first time it appears, and define technical terms briefly.
Write values that are not known yet as a bracketed placeholder, for example “[source]”. A narrative that contains placeholders is a draft.
Avoid wording that implies criticism of colleagues or of earlier workflows.

title: Methodology Narrative Standard
text:
Narratives and code
The narrative is the specification. When the code and the narrative disagree, the disagreement is reported and recorded in the drift log (validation_log in the schema), not quietly reconciled in either direction. The plain-language description produced from the code by the narrator tool is compared against the narrative for this purpose.

The source lead writes the narrative.
[Open] Who reviews and approves it, and what status values a narrative carries (for example draft, under review, approved).
Changes to an approved narrative are made through Git, so every change has an author and a date.
When this standard changes, its version number goes up. Each narrative records the version it follows, and the custom AI tools are updated to match.

title: Schema
text:
The schema is five related tables in schema/. They record what the inventory estimates, what data each estimate needs, how that data is obtained, which data dictionary governs each dataset, and where the pipeline has drifted from the methodology. The CSV files are edited by hand. R/build_schema_parquet.R converts them to Parquet in schema/parquet/ and validates the Parquet against schema/data-dict.yaml with the data-dict command-line tool. That dictionary is the full column-level reference, including allowed values and the rules each table must satisfy; the tables below summarize it. Columns marked as lists hold semicolon-separated values in the CSV file. To load and query the schema, see Query the schema.
For a browsable version of the dictionary, with a diagram of how the tables relate, a searchable list of every column, and summaries of the current data, open the schema data dictionary page. It is a single file that works offline, so it can also be copied to a shared drive or attached to an email.

text: This document records the design decisions behind the GHGI pipeline and the reasons for them, so that future contributors, human or automated, can follow the intent behind the code.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text: This document records the design decisions behind the GHGI pipeline and the reasons for them, so that future contributors, human or automated, can follow the intent behind the code.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text:
Narrative as specification
Domain experts write plain-language methodology narratives for each source category. These narratives are the specification. A chain of three custom tools turns them into code and back into readable documentation:

A methodology parser converts a narrative into a structured, step-by-step implementation framework, without writing any code.
An R coder turns that framework into R code that follows the project’s conventions.
A methodology narrator translates finished R code back into a plain-language description that experts can review even if they do not read R.

The distinctive feature of this approach is that the specifications are written by domain experts, not programmers, and the work is tied to regulatory accountability. Human judgment sits at the design stage and at review checkpoints, and the tools follow the specification.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text:
Principles
Fail loudly, not silently. Missing inputs, unrecognized units, and ambiguous steps must stop the pipeline with a clear error. A plausible guess in a compliance inventory is worse than no answer.
Drift is signal. The specification layer and the code layer are kept separate on purpose. When they disagree, the disagreement is reported. Two real examples: a discontinued data source is still live in the code, and the code uses MOVES3 while the 2026 report cites MOVES5.
Canonical units at ingestion, conversion at output. Converting once at the boundary, and nowhere else, means a unit error can only enter at two well-defined places, both of which are checked. Calculations in between stay unitless and easy to audit. The detailed rules are under Unit discipline in AGENTS.md.
The meta-module is a control plane. The narratives and the schema should generate and constrain the pipeline, not merely sit beside it as documentation.
Pilot first. Each pattern is proven on one source category before it is applied more widely, with a human review at each step.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text:
Ordering decisions to make early
Two choices constrain everything built afterward and are easy to postpone by mistake:

The convention for representing uncertainty must be settled before ingestion is built. This supersedes an earlier plan to defer uncertainty analysis (Monte Carlo simulation) to a later phase. Whether the convention relies on EPA’s published uncertainty ranges or propagates probability distributions through the calculations is part of this decision.
The schema for the emissions store should be frozen earlier than it feels necessary.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text:
Where the effort goes
Writing specifications is the main bottleneck, more than writing code. Adding contractors does not relieve it, because the expertise required is the scarce resource. The AI tool chain absorbs much of the work that would otherwise be contracted out.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
section: Why a hub and separate source-category repositories
text:
Why a hub and separate source-category repositories
Work is split between this coordination hub and one repository per sector. The hub holds everything that must be shared and agreed once: the schema registry, the methodology narratives, cross-cutting rules, and conventions. Each source-category repository holds only the data pulling, transformation, calculation, and visualization for its sector. This keeps sector leads’ work independent while guaranteeing that every sector reads the same categories, datasets, and boundary rules. {syrinx} is installed as a package rather than copied into each repository for the same reason: one shared implementation, one place to fix it.
The list of repositories and the standard source-category layout are under Repository structure in AGENTS.md.

title: GHGI Architecture and Design Principles
text:
Open decisions
These decisions are deliberately left open. Who makes each kind of decision is set out under Decision authority in AGENTS.md. Months are counted from project start. [Confirm the start date.]

Pipeline orchestration with {targets}
The current approach is numbered sequential scripts (01_download.R, 02_clean.R, and so on). Consider adopting {targets} when scripts develop many interdependencies, full rebuilds take too long, intermediate results need caching, or several people contribute to the same pipeline. The questions to ask are whether running scripts by hand is becoming error-prone, whether expensive calculations are being re-run unnecessarily, and whether the benefit justifies the learning curve. Re-evaluate after the minimum viable product, around Month 4. Calculation functions are already written so they can become {targets} steps, so adopting it later means adding tar_target() calls, not rewriting functions.


Testing depth
The current approach is basic unit tests for calculation functions. Data validation at ingestion and output is already required, so the open question is whether to add integration tests and benchmark tests. Consider expanding when bugs reach production, when new team members join, or before external review. Decide by Month 3, based on how often bugs appear.


Central data acquisition hub
The current approach is manual downloads, sector by sector. A central hub would hold one download wrapper per provider (for example EIA, the EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, and USDA NASS), automated update checks, versioned raw data, notification when new data is released, and download logs as an audit trail. The dataset registry in schema/ghgi_datasets.csv already records each dataset’s access method and endpoint, and retrieval_plan() groups datasets by access method, so the registry would drive the hub. Consider building it when manual downloads become a bottleneck, missed updates cause delays, several sectors share the same sources, or provenance tracking becomes a requirement. It depends on established API access with the agencies and agreement on update frequency. Design around Month 7 and pilot in Months 10 to 12.


Public data portal
Options are an interactive Shiny dashboard, an API for programmatic access, a static website with documentation and download links, or a combination. Consider it once the inventory is stable and validated, external users are asking for data, and the work is ready for public scrutiny. Not before Month 12.


Criteria for adding complexity
Before adding a tool or process, ask:

Does the current simple approach actually cause problems? If not, do not add complexity.
What does the status quo cost in time, errors, or missed opportunities?
What does the new approach cost in learning curve, maintenance, and technical debt?
Who benefits, how often, and is the benefit critical or merely convenient?
Is the change reversible, and what would it lock in?
Is there time, skill, and bandwidth to implement and maintain it?



Review milestones

Month 3: Is the storage approach (Parquet with {pins}) working? Is {syrinx} proving valuable? Are the separate GitHub repositories effective? Does the course need adjusting?
Month 6: Is a central data hub needed? Is the testing strategy adequate? Is workflow orchestration needed?
Month 12: Is the system meeting its goals? Which future capabilities come next? What resources are needed for Year 2? What is the external engagement strategy?

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
These notes explain data-availability risks, retrieval difficulty, and known recent-year gaps for each sector. They were collected from the former sector boundary notes. They are context, not rules: the rules for which sector reports each emission are in Cross-Sector Boundary Rules.
Most notes are category-specific and could eventually move to the relevant source-category repository. The data-availability lists could instead be generated from schema/ghgi_datasets.csv, for example with at_risk_sources() (see Query the schema).

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
Energy

Availability risk: Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) Subparts W (petroleum and natural gas systems), FF (coal), and RR/UU (CO2 injection) all have source_status = uncertain. DS-EPA-CMOP and DS-EPA-MSW-COMBUST are EPA programs with uncertain continuity.
Hard to retrieve: DS-ENVERUS-WELLS requires a commercial license. DS-STATE-WELLS comes from many state oil and gas commissions with no single feed, and is the hardest abandoned-well activity data to assemble.
Easier to retrieve: EIA Open Data v2 covers coal, natural gas, and petroleum throughput through the same API client as the fossil fuel combustion fetcher. The MSHA Mine Data Retrieval System is a public CSV download.
Fossil fuel combustion was mapped and reconciled against the existing _targets.R. The reconciliation identified four differences between code and chapter: Fuel Oil and Kerosene Sales (FOKS) method drift, Motor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) version drift, the GHGRP disaggregation structure, and state and territory scope. The dataset_provenance.csv file that originally recorded these was retired as duplicative.

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
IPPU

GHGRP is the dominant IPPU activity-data source. Many values are aggregated confidential business information (ammonia, nitric acid, lime, cement, petrochemicals, CO2 consumption, urea). All GHGRP-dependent IPPU categories inherit source_status = uncertain.
The USGS National Minerals Information Center publishes per-commodity files for minerals and metals.
Industry associations (AISI, ACC, AHRI, TFI, USAA, NLA) are membership or manual sources and need manual retrieval.
ODS substitutes, the largest IPPU source, are driven by the EPA Vintaging Model, a bottom-up stock model rather than a downloadable dataset. Continuity of its output is uncertain.
CARB SF6 data informs the non-reporter emission factor for electrical equipment.
Reconciliation: the four ippu_dist_* targets in the existing _targets.R (ammonia, petrochemicals, carbon black, iron and steel) are the Energy side of the feedstock reallocation, and the IPPU chapter is the receiving side. The rule above lists seven receiving sources, so aluminum, titanium dioxide, and zinc have no matching target yet. An end-to-end trace should confirm the reallocation reconciles.

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
Agriculture

Hard to retrieve: DS-USDA-NRI is proprietary and underlies DayCent. DS-DAYCENT-OUTPUT is model output available only via EPA 2025 (FOIA), with uncertain continuity. DS-IFA-FERTILIZER (IFASTAT) is membership-gated for the full series. DS-BURNED-AREA is an EPA-derived six-state analysis, extrapolated, with no clean public feed.
Easier to retrieve: the USDA NASS QuickStats API covers enteric fermentation, manure, rice, soils surrogate data, and field burning activity data through one endpoint. PRISM precipitation and USGS crushed stone are straightforward downloads.

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
LULUCF

Land representation: three databases (NRI for non-federal land, FIA for forest, NLCD for federal land and Alaska) classify the 936 million hectare U.S. land base into 36 IPCC land-use and land-use-change categories. FIA is authoritative for forest; NRI and NLCD are adjusted to match.
Only managed land is inventoried (886 of 936 million hectares). The managed-land designation uses PAD-US, USFS TPO (timber), NASS county grazing data, and EIA and USGS resource-extraction data, so several datasets feed the land base before any flux calculation.
Hard to retrieve: DS-USDA-NRI is the most load-bearing LULUCF input (cropland, grassland, settlements, conversions, land base); it is proprietary and runs through 2017 only. DS-DAYCENT-LULUCF is Tier 3 model output via EPA 2025 (FOIA) with uncertain continuity. DS-NRCS-CEAP is a restricted management survey. DS-OPTIS is a proprietary remote-sensing product.
DayCent underlies both agricultural soils (Ch. 5.4) and cropland and grassland soil carbon here: one dependency, two sectors. The registry records it as two datasets, DS-DAYCENT-OUTPUT and DS-DAYCENT-LULUCF.
Easier to retrieve: USFS FIA DataMart (forest, harvested wood products, urban trees); NLCD, NOAA C-CAP, MTBS, and PAD-US geospatial downloads; and the NID public API for reservoir surface area.
Some leaf categories (peatlands, land converted to other land) are flagged needs_validation pending the GHGIA chapter’s exact treatment.

title: Sector Data Notes
text:
Waste
Recent-year (2024) data gaps worth tracking as provenance:

MSW landfills: 2024 GHGRP data were not available at preparation time, so 2023 net emissions and derived parameters are held constant.
Composting: 2019–2024 tonnage is extrapolated from the 2018 per-capita ratio times Census population.
Anaerobic digestion: 1990–2015, 2020–2021, and 2024 rely on extrapolation or interpolation; 2024 is approximated by averaging 2022–2023 survey data.
The BioCycle State of Garbage survey (historical MSW activity data) is discontinued.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Scope
This category covers methane and nitrous oxide from the treatment and discharge of domestic and industrial wastewater, in two sources:

Domestic wastewater (domestic_wastewater): wastewater from residential and commercial sources, treated at publicly owned treatment works (POTWs) or in septic systems, plus emissions from treated effluent discharged to receiving waters.
Industrial wastewater (industrial_wastewater): wastewater with a high organic load that industries treat on site. It covers breweries, ethanol production, pulp and paper, meat and poultry, petroleum refining, and fruit and vegetable processing.

It does not cover:

Biogenic carbon dioxide from wastewater, which is excluded from national totals by convention.
Methane recovered and combusted for energy. It is subtracted from this category’s emissions (steps 4 and 6).
Emissions from biosolids once they leave the treatment system (see Connections to other categories).

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Emission factors and other constants

bod_per_capita: [value] kilograms of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) per person per day. Source: [reference] (DS-WW-EF). Years: all.
mcf_[pathway]: the methane correction factor for each treatment pathway (aerobic, anaerobic, septic, constructed wetlands, and discharge), meaning the degree to which conditions are anaerobic. [values], unitless. Source: [reference].
ch4_max_bod: [value] kilograms of CH₄ per kilogram of BOD, the maximum methane-producing capacity. Source: [reference].
cod_per_unit_[industry] and ww_per_unit_[industry]: chemical oxygen demand (COD) per unit of wastewater, and wastewater generated per unit of production, for each industry. [values], in [industry-specific units]. Source: [reference].
ch4_max_cod: [value] kilograms of CH₄ per kilogram of COD. Source: [reference].
n2o_ef_effluent: [value] kilograms of N₂O-nitrogen per kilogram of nitrogen discharged. Source: [reference].
n2o_ef_[industry]: N₂O emission factors for the industries estimated for N₂O. [values]. Source: [reference].
n_fraction_protein: [value] kilograms of nitrogen per kilogram of protein. Source: [reference].
Species conversion ratio: 44/28 converts N₂O-nitrogen to N₂O. It is a conversion ratio, not an emission factor.
Global warming potentials: AR5, for CH₄ and N₂O.

title: Example Methodology Narrative: Wastewater Treatment (CH₄ and N₂O)
text:
Calculation steps

Domestic organic load. From population (DS-CENSUS-POP) and bod_per_capita, estimate the annual domestic BOD load. Split it between septic and centralized treatment using the household shares (DS-CENSUS-AHS), and split the centralized part across treatment pathways using the pathway flows ([not registered]). Output: BOD load by pathway and year.
Tertiary flow. Estimate the share of centralized flow receiving tertiary treatment (constructed wetlands). Where direct figures are not available, fit the share from historical data (see Rules and judgment calls). Output: tertiary share by year, applied to step 1’s pathway split.
Domestic CH₄. For each pathway, and for discharged effluent, CH₄ equals BOD load × ch4_max_bod × mcf_[pathway]. Sum across pathways. Output: gross domestic CH₄ by year.
Domestic energy recovery. Forecast POTW anaerobic digester flow for years beyond the available data (see Rules and judgment calls), estimate the methane recovered and combusted, and subtract it from step 3’s total. Output: net domestic CH₄ by year.
Domestic N₂O. Derive the nitrogen load in effluent from available protein (DS-FAO-FBS), protein consumption ([not registered]), population, and n_fraction_protein. N₂O equals nitrogen load × n2o_ef_effluent × 44/28. Output: domestic N₂O by year.
Industrial CH₄ and N₂O. For each industry, wastewater equals production (from that industry’s dataset) × ww_per_unit_[industry], and organic load equals wastewater × cod_per_unit_[industry]. CH₄ equals organic load × ch4_max_cod × the methane correction factor for the industry’s treatment, minus any methane recovered. For industries estimated for N₂O, apply n2o_ef_[industry]. Output: CH₄, and N₂O where applicable, by industry and year.
Aggregate. Sum domestic and industrial CH₄, and domestic and industrial N₂O. Output: category CH₄ and N₂O by year.
Carbon dioxide equivalent. Multiply each gas by its AR5 global warming potential. Output: category totals in carbon dioxide equivalent by year.
